subject: pe
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which mechanism does NOT aid venous return during exercise?
questions.explain: Venous return is aided by the muscle pump, respiratory pump and valves, not by increased viscosity.

questions.q: A motor unit is best defined as:
options: A group of muscles working as antagonists
A motor neurone and all the muscle fibres it stimulates
A single muscle fibre and its mitochondria
questions.explain: A motor unit comprises a single motor neurone and all the muscle fibres it innervates.

questions.q: Which best describes the relationship within the energy continuum?
options: All three systems contribute, with the predominant one depending on intensity and duration
The aerobic system is never used in team games
Only one system ever works at a time
Anaerobic systems supply all marathon energy
questions.explain: The energy continuum means all three systems contribute simultaneously, with the dominant one set by exercise intensity and duration.

questions.q: The aerobic energy system's high ATP yield comes mainly from:
options: The cori cycle in the liver
The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain in the mitochondria
questions.explain: The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain in the mitochondria yield the majority of aerobic ATP.

questions.q: Cardiac output is correctly calculated as:
questions.explain: Cardiac output (Q) equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

questions.q: Which muscle-fibre type is best suited to a marathon runner?
questions.explain: Type I slow oxidative fibres are highly fatigue-resistant and aerobic, ideal for endurance events.

questions.q: Starling's law of the heart states that stroke volume increases when there is greater:
options: Sympathetic stimulation of the SA node
questions.explain: Greater venous return stretches the ventricle walls, increasing the force of contraction and stroke volume.

questions.q: Performing prolonged exercise in hot conditions primarily challenges the body by:
options: Causing dehydration and competing demands for blood flow between muscles and skin
questions.explain: In the heat, blood is diverted to the skin for cooling while muscles also demand it, and sweating risks dehydration.

questions.q: The 'all-or-none' law of muscle contraction means that:
options: All muscle fibres in the body contract together
Force is graded within a single fibre
If a motor unit fires, all its fibres contract maximally
questions.explain: When a motor unit is stimulated above threshold, all of its fibres contract maximally, or none do.

questions.q: As blood passes through a respiring muscle, the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the right. This Bohr shift is caused by:
options: Increased CO2, lower pH and higher temperature
questions.explain: The Bohr shift results from raised CO2, lowered pH and increased temperature, releasing more oxygen to muscles.

questions.q: The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve has an S (sigmoid) shape. A shift to the RIGHT means haemoglobin:
options: Has a greater affinity for oxygen
Binds more oxygen at the lungs
Releases oxygen more readily to tissues
questions.explain: A right shift lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so oxygen is unloaded more readily at the tissues.

questions.q: During steady submaximal exercise, the term 'a-vO2 difference' refers to:
options: The difference in oxygen content between arterial and venous blood
The difference in pressure between atria and ventricles
questions.explain: The arterio-venous oxygen difference is the difference in oxygen content between arterial and mixed venous blood, indicating oxygen extraction.

questions.q: The ATP-PC (alactic) energy system regenerates ATP using:
options: Phosphocreatine broken down by creatine kinase
questions.explain: Creatine kinase breaks down phosphocreatine to resynthesise ATP rapidly without oxygen.

questions.q: EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) fast component is mainly used to:
options: Remove all lactic acid from blood
Resaturate myoglobin and replenish ATP and PC stores
questions.explain: The fast (alactacid) component restores ATP and PC stores and resaturates myoglobin with oxygen.

questions.q: Gaseous exchange at the alveoli occurs by:
questions.explain: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the alveolar membrane down their respective partial pressure gradients.

questions.q: A buffering agent such as sodium bicarbonate is used by athletes to:
options: Neutralise hydrogen ions and delay the effects of lactic acid
questions.explain: Bicarbonate raises blood buffering capacity, reducing acidity and delaying fatigue from lactate accumulation.

questions.q: Myoglobin's main role in muscle is to:
options: Store and transport oxygen within the muscle fibre
questions.explain: Myoglobin stores oxygen in muscle and releases it to the mitochondria for aerobic respiration.

questions.q: For a power athlete loading before competition, the most appropriate dietary manipulation is:
options: Creatine supplementation to boost PC stores
Carbohydrate loading over three days with depletion
questions.explain: Creatine supplementation increases phosphocreatine stores, benefiting short, high-intensity power efforts.

questions.q: Which structure of the heart's conduction system acts as the pacemaker, initiating the cardiac impulse?
questions.explain: The sinoatrial node spontaneously generates the impulse and sets the heart rate.

questions.q: Which respiratory adaptation results from long-term aerobic training?
options: Increased strength of respiratory muscles and greater gas exchange efficiency
questions.explain: Training strengthens respiratory muscles and improves the efficiency of pulmonary gas exchange.

questions.q: Glycogen (carbohydrate) loading is most beneficial for an athlete competing in:
options: A prolonged endurance event such as a marathon
questions.explain: Carbohydrate loading maximises glycogen stores, delaying fatigue in prolonged aerobic endurance events.

questions.q: Vascular shunting (the vascular shunt mechanism) during exercise involves:
options: Vasoconstriction to all body tissues equally
Closing of the capillary beds at the muscles
Vasodilation to muscles and vasoconstriction to the gut and non-essential organs
questions.explain: Arterioles supplying working muscles vasodilate while those to non-essential organs vasoconstrict, redirecting blood flow.

questions.q: During a 100 m sprint lasting around 10 seconds, the predominant energy system is the:
questions.explain: Maximal efforts up to about 10 seconds are fuelled predominantly by the ATP-PC system.

questions.q: Which ion is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum to trigger muscle contraction?
questions.explain: Calcium ions bind to troponin, moving tropomyosin and exposing actin binding sites for cross-bridge formation.

questions.q: A chronic cardiovascular adaptation to endurance training is:
options: Cardiac hypertrophy and increased resting stroke volume
questions.explain: Endurance training enlarges the heart (hypertrophy), raising stroke volume and lowering resting heart rate (bradycardia).

questions.q: During the cardiac conduction sequence, after the AV node the impulse passes to the:
questions.explain: The impulse passes from the AV node down the bundle of His before reaching the Purkinje fibres.

questions.q: At altitude, the reduced partial pressure of oxygen leads to a chronic adaptation of:
options: Increased red blood cell and haemoglobin production
questions.explain: Hypoxia at altitude stimulates EPO release, increasing red blood cell and haemoglobin concentration over time.

questions.q: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a banned ergogenic aid because it:
options: Stimulates red blood cell production, increasing oxygen-carrying capacity
questions.explain: EPO increases erythrocyte production, raising oxygen transport, but also dangerously increases blood viscosity.

questions.q: According to the sliding-filament theory, muscle shortening occurs when:
options: Actin filaments slide over myosin, pulled by cross-bridges
questions.explain: Myosin cross-bridges attach to actin and pull the actin filaments inwards, shortening the sarcomere.

questions.q: A by-product of the anaerobic glycolytic system that contributes to fatigue is:
questions.explain: Anaerobic glycolysis produces lactic acid, lowering pH and contributing to muscular fatigue.
